column2: And there came a public beggar, who through the town
used to beg in Ithaca, and was conspicuous for his ravenous belly,
for eating and drinking without stop; and he had no strength
nor might, but in size he was very big to look upon.
Arnaeus was his name; for his lady mother gave it
from birth; but Irus all the young men called him,
because he used to carry messages, going, whenever anyone might bid him;
who, coming, was driving Odysseus from his own house,
and, reviling him, addressed him with winged words:

Give way, old man, from the porch, lest soon you be dragged even by the foot.
11	Do you not hear that all are winking at me,
12	and bid me drag you? But I am ashamed all the same.
13	Come, up with you, lest soon strife between us two come even to blows.
Then looking darkly at him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Strange man, I do you no harm, nor do I speak any,
16	nor do I grudge anyone giving, even if he took up much.
17	This threshold will hold us both, and you have no need
18	to be jealous of others' goods; for you seem to me to be a wanderer
19	just like me, and prosperity the gods are likely to bestow.
20	But do not challenge me too much with your hands, lest you anger me,
21	lest, old though I am, I smear your chest and lips
22	with blood; and I would have quiet even more
23	tomorrow; for I do not think you will return
24	a second time to the hall of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
Then, enraged, Irus the beggar spoke to him:

Oh, how the filthy glutton chatters on glibly,
27	like an old woman, a furnace-keeper; whom I would plan evil for,
28	striking with both hands, and on the ground all his teeth
29	I would knock out of his jaws, like a pig's that ravages the crops.
30	Gird yourself now, that all these too may know
31	us fighting; but how would you fight with a younger man?
So they in front of the high doors
on the polished threshold were stirring each other up with all their heart.
And the sacred might of Antinous perceived the two,
and laughing sweetly he spoke among the suitors:

O friends, never before has such a thing come about,
37	such a delight a god has brought to this house.
38	The stranger and Irus are contending with each other
39	to fight with their hands; come, let us set them on quickly.
So he spoke, and they all leapt up laughing,
and gathered round the ill-clad beggars.
And among them spoke Antinous, son of Eupeithes:

Hear me, proud suitors, that I may say something.
44	These paunches of goats lie on the fire, which for supper
45	we put there, having filled them with fat and blood;
46	and whichever of the two wins and proves the stronger,
47	let him rise and himself take whichever of these he wishes;
48	and he shall always feast with us, nor shall we allow any other
49	beggar to mix inside with us to beg.
So spoke Antinous, and the speech pleased them.
And among them, planning guile, spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O friends, in no way is it possible for an older man to fight
53	with a younger, a man worn down by misery; but my belly
54	urges me on, the evil-doer, that I may be beaten by blows.
55	But come now, all of you swear me a mighty oath,
56	that no one, to favour Irus, with a heavy hand
57	strike me wantonly, and by force subdue me for this man.
So he spoke, and they all swore as he bade.
But when they had sworn and had finished the oath,
then among them spoke again the sacred might of Telemachus:

Stranger, if your heart and proud spirit urge you
62	to defend yourself against this man, fear none of the other Achaeans,
63	since he will fight with many who strikes you;
64	I am your host, and the kings approve,
65	Antinous and Eurymachus, both prudent men.
So he spoke, and all approved; and Odysseus
girded his rags about his loins, and showed his thighs,
fair and great, and his broad shoulders showed,
and his chest and strong arms; and Athena
standing close by made the limbs of the shepherd of the people grow big.
And the suitors all marvelled exceedingly;
and thus one would say, looking at his neighbour:

Surely soon Irus, Non-Irus (Airos), will have a self-drawn evil, // pun: Ἶρος Ἄϊρος
74	such a thigh from his rags the old man shows.
So they spoke, and the spirit of Irus was badly stirred.
But even so the servants, having girded him, led him by force,
afraid; and the flesh trembled on his limbs.
And Antinous rebuked him, and spoke a word and called him by name:

Now would you were not, you bull-boaster, nor had been born,
80	if indeed you tremble at this man and fear him terribly,
81	an old man, worn down by misery which comes upon him.
82	But I will tell you, and it shall also be accomplished:
83	if this man defeats you and proves the stronger,
84	I will send you to the mainland, throwing you in a black ship,
85	to king Echetus, the harmer of all mortals,
86	who will cut off your nose and ears with pitiless bronze,
87	and drag out your privy parts and give them raw to dogs to tear.
So he spoke, and still more trembling seized his limbs.
And they led him into the middle; and both raised their hands.
Then the much-enduring godly Odysseus pondered
whether to strike him so that his life would leave him as he fell on the spot,
or strike him gently and stretch him on the ground.
And as he thought, this seemed to him the better course,
to strike gently, that the Achaeans might not notice him.
Then, the two raising their hands, one struck the right shoulder,
Irus, and the other struck the neck beneath the ear, and the bones within
he crushed; and at once red blood came along his mouth,
and he fell in the dust bellowing, and gnashed his teeth,
kicking the ground with his feet; and the noble suitors,
raising their hands, died of laughter. But Odysseus
dragged him out through the porch, taking him by the foot, till he came to the courtyard
and the gate of the portico; and by the wall of the courtyard
he sat him leaning him back; and put a staff in his hand,
and speaking to him addressed him with winged words:

Sit here now, keeping off the swine and dogs,
106	and do not be lord of strangers and beggars,
107	wretch that you are, lest you get some worse evil still.
He spoke, and about his shoulders he threw his unseemly wallet,
full of holes; and in it was a twisted cord for a strap.
And back to the threshold he went and sat down; and they went inside
sweetly laughing and mocking with words:

May Zeus give you, stranger, and the other immortal gods,
113	what you most wish and what is dear to your heart,
114	you who have made this insatiable fellow stop begging
115	in the district; for soon we shall take him to the mainland,
116	to king Echetus, the harmer of all mortals.
So they spoke, and godly Odysseus rejoiced at the omen.
And Antinous set beside him a great paunch,
full of fat and blood; and Amphinomus
took up two loaves from the basket and set them beside him,
and pledged him with a golden cup, and spoke:

Hail, father stranger; may prosperity be yours hereafter;
123	but now at least you are held in many evils.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Amphinomus, you seem to me indeed very prudent;
126	for such also was your father, since I heard a good report,
127	Nisus of Dulichium, that he was both good and wealthy;
128	from him they say you were born, and you seem a man of fair speech.
129	Therefore I will tell you, and do you mark and listen to me:
130	nothing feebler does the earth nourish than man,
131	of all things that on the earth breathe and creep.
132	For he says he will never suffer evil hereafter,
133	so long as the gods give him prowess and his knees are lively;
134	but when the blessed gods bring even sad things to pass,
135	these too he bears unwillingly with an enduring spirit;
136	for such is the mind of men upon the earth
137	as the day which the father of men and gods brings on.
138	For I too was once to be prosperous among men,
139	and I did many wanton deeds, yielding to violence and power,
140	trusting in my father and my brothers.
141	Therefore let no man ever be lawless altogether,
142	but let him hold the gifts of the gods in silence, whatever they give.
143	Such things I see the suitors, devising wanton acts,
144	wasting the possessions and dishonouring the wife
145	of a man who, I say, will no longer be far from his friends
146	and native land for long; indeed very near. But may a god
147	lead you away homeward, and may you not meet him,
148	when he comes back to his dear native land;
149	for I think the suitors and he will not be parted
150	without blood, once he comes beneath the roof.
So he spoke, and pouring a libation drank the honey-sweet wine,
and put the cup back into the hands of the marshaller of the people.
But he went through the house, grieved at heart,
nodding his head; for his spirit foreboded evil.
But not even so did he escape fate; for Athena bound him too
to be overcome by the hands and spear of Telemachus.
And again he sat down on the chair from which he had risen.
And in her mind the goddess grey-eyed Athena put it,
to the daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope,
to appear to the suitors, that she might most open out
the hearts of the suitors and become honoured
more by her husband and son than before.
And she laughed without cause and spoke a word and called by name:

Eurynome, my heart longs, though not before at all,
165	to appear to the suitors, hateful though they are all the same;
166	and to my son I would say a word, which would be better,
167	not to mix with all the overweening suitors,
168	who speak fair, but think ill behind.
Then to her in turn spoke the housekeeper Eurynome:

Yes indeed, child, all this you have said in due measure.
171	But go and tell your son the word, and hide nothing,
172	having washed your skin and anointed your cheeks;
173	and do not go thus with your face stained all over with tears,
174	since it is worse to grieve unceasingly.
175	For already your son is of such age, whom above all
176	you prayed to the immortals to see with a beard.
Then wise Penelope spoke to her in turn:

Eurynome, do not urge this, though you are kind,
179	to wash my skin and anoint myself with oil;
180	for my beauty the gods who hold Olympus
181	destroyed, from the time he went in the hollow ships.
182	But bid Autonoe and Hippodameia
183	come, that they may stand beside me in the halls;
184	alone I will not go among the men; for I am ashamed.
So she spoke, and the old woman went through the hall
to tell the women and urge them to come.
Then again the goddess grey-eyed Athena thought of other things:
on the daughter of Icarius she poured sweet sleep,
and she slept, reclining, and all her limbs were loosed
there on the couch; and meanwhile the divine one among goddesses
gave immortal gifts, that the Achaeans might admire her.
First with beauty she cleansed her fair face
with ambrosial stuff, such as the fair-crowned Cytherea
anoints herself with, when she goes to the lovely dance of the Graces;
and she made her taller and stouter to look upon,
and she made her whiter than sawn ivory.
Having so done, the divine one among goddesses departed,
and the white-armed handmaids came from the hall
coming with a noise; and sweet sleep released her,
and she wiped her cheeks with her hands and spoke:

Truly a soft slumber has covered me, very miserable though I am.
202	Would that pure Artemis would give me so soft a death
203	right now, that no longer grieving in my heart
204	I may waste my life away, longing for my dear husband's
205	every excellence, since he was outstanding among the Achaeans.
So saying she came down from the shining upper chamber,
not alone; with her two handmaids followed.
And when she, the divine one among women, came to the suitors,
she stood by the post of the strongly built roof,
holding before her cheeks her shining veil;
and a faithful handmaid stood on either side of her.
Their knees were loosened on the spot, and their hearts were bewitched by desire,
and all prayed to lie beside her in bed.
And she addressed Telemachus, her dear son:

Telemachus, your wits are no longer steady, nor your thought;
216	as a child you used to turn over shrewd designs in your mind more;
217	but now, when you are big and have reached the measure of youth,
218	and anyone, looking to your size and beauty, a stranger,
219	would say you are the offspring of a prosperous man,
220	no longer are your wits right, nor your thought.
221	What a deed this has been done in the halls,
222	that you allowed the stranger to be so mistreated.
223	How is it now, if a stranger sitting in our house
224	thus suffers from a painful scuffle?
225	For you shame and disgrace would arise among men.
Then prudent Telemachus answered her:

My mother, that you are angry I do not blame you;
228	but I understand in my heart and know each thing,
229	the good and the worse; before I was still a child.
230	But I cannot think everything prudently;
231	for they strike me, sitting by, one from one side, another from another,
232	these men with evil thoughts, and I have no helpers.
233	Yet the match of the stranger and Irus did not come about
234	by the will of the suitors, but the stranger was stronger in might.
235	Would that, father Zeus and Athena and Apollo,
236	so now the suitors in our house
237	might nod their heads, overcome, some in the courtyard,
238	some inside the house, and the limbs of each be loosed,
239	as now that Irus at the courtyard doors
240	sits nodding his head, like one drunk,
241	and cannot stand upright on his feet nor go
242	home, where his return is, since his dear limbs are loosened.
So they spoke such things to one another;
and Eurymachus addressed Penelope with words:

Daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope,
246	if all the Achaeans in Iasian Argos could see you,
247	more suitors in your house
248	would feast from dawn, since you surpass women
249	in form and stature and in well-balanced wits within.
Then wise Penelope answered him:

Eurymachus, my excellence and form and figure
252	the immortals destroyed, when the Argives went up
253	to Ilium, and among them went my husband Odysseus.
254	If he, coming, were to tend my life,
255	greater would be my fame and fairer so.
256	But now I grieve; so many evils has a god heaped on me.
257	Indeed when he went, leaving the native land,
258	taking me by the right hand at the wrist, he said:
259	'Wife, I do not think that the well-greaved Achaeans
260	will all return unharmed from Troy;
261	for they say the Trojans are warrior men,
262	both javelin-throwers and drawers of arrows,
263	and mounters of swift-footed horses, which most quickly
264	decide the great strife of even war.
265	Therefore I do not know whether a god will let me return, or whether I shall be taken
266	there in Troy; but here let everything be your care.
267	Remember my father and mother in the halls
268	as now, or even more, while I am away;
269	but when you see our son with a beard,
270	marry whom you wish, leaving your house.'
271	Thus he spoke; and now all this is being accomplished.
272	The night will come when a hateful marriage will meet
273	me, ill-fated, of whom Zeus has taken away happiness.
274	But this dread grief comes upon my heart and spirit:
275	this was not the custom of suitors before;
276	those who wish to woo a good woman and the daughter of a rich man
277	and compete with one another,
278	themselves bring oxen and fat sheep,
279	a feast for the girl's friends, and give splendid gifts;
280	but do not eat another's livelihood without payment.
So she spoke, and the much-enduring godly Odysseus was glad,
because she drew gifts from them, and charmed their spirit
with honeyed words, but her mind intended other things.
Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke to her in turn:

Daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope,
286	gifts, whichever of the Achaeans wishes to bring here,
287	accept; for it is not good to refuse a gift;
288	but we shall not go to our works before, nor anywhere else,
289	until you marry whichever of the Achaeans is best.
So spoke Antinous, and the speech pleased them;
and each sent a herald to bring gifts.
For Antinous he brought a great, very beautiful robe,
embroidered; and in it were twelve brooches, all
golden, fitted with well-bent clasps.
For Eurymachus he brought at once a much-wrought necklace,
golden, strung with amber, like the sun.
Two attendants brought earrings for Eurydamas,
three-drop mulberry-shaped; much grace shone from them.
And from the lord Pisander, son of Polyctor,
an attendant brought a necklace, a very beautiful ornament.
And another of the Achaeans brought another fair gift.
Then she went up to the upper chamber, divine among women,
and with her the handmaids carried the very beautiful gifts.
And they, turning to dance and lovely song,
took their pleasure, and waited for evening to come.
And as they took their pleasure, black evening came upon them.
At once they set up three braziers in the hall,
to give light; and around them they put dry wood,
dry long ago, hard, newly split with bronze,
and they mixed in torches; and in turn they kept them alight,
the maidservants of enduring Odysseus. But he
himself, the Zeus-born, Odysseus of many wiles, spoke among them:

Maidservants of Odysseus, the lord long gone,
314	go to the chamber, where the revered queen is;
315	and beside her spin the distaffs, and please her
316	sitting in the hall, or card the wool with your hands;
317	but I will provide light for all these.
318	For even if they wish to wait for fair-throned Dawn,
319	they will not defeat me; I am very much-enduring.
So he spoke, and they laughed, and looked at one another.
And fair-cheeked Melantho rebuked him shamefully,
whom Dolius begot, and Penelope brought up,
and tended as a child, and gave her toys to please her heart;
but not even so did she have grief in her mind for Penelope,
but she consorted with Eurymachus and was his lover.
She reviled Odysseus with words of reproach:

Wretched stranger, you are someone struck out of his wits,
328	and you do not wish to go to sleep in a smithy,
329	or in some meeting-place, but here you talk much,
330	boldly among many men, and in your heart you are not at all
331	afraid; surely wine holds your wits, or always
332	such is your mind; so that you also babble vainly.
333	Are you out of your senses because you beat Irus the beggar?
334	Beware lest soon someone better than Irus rise up,
335	who, smashing you about the head with strong hands,
336	will send you out of the house, befouling you with much blood.
Then looking darkly at her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Soon I shall tell Telemachus, bitch, what you say,
339	going there, that he may cut you limb from limb on the spot.
So saying he scared the women with his words.
and they went off through the house, and the limbs of each were loosed
with fear; for they thought he spoke the truth.
But he, by the blazing braziers giving light,
stood looking at them all; and his heart
was pondering other things in his mind, which did not go unfulfilled.
But Athena did not let the proud suitors at all
refrain from heart-grieving insult, so that still more
pain might sink into the heart of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
And among them Eurymachus, son of Polybus, began to speak,
mocking Odysseus; and he made laughter for his comrades:

Hear me, suitors of the famous queen,
352	that I may say what the spirit in my breast bids me.
353	Not without a god has this man come to the house of Odysseus;
354	at any rate it seems to me the gleam of torches comes from him,
355	from his head, since there are no hairs on it, not even a few.
He spoke, and at once addressed Odysseus, sacker of cities:

Stranger, would you be willing to work for hire, if I took you on,
358	at the edge of a farm—and your pay shall be sure—
359	gathering stones for walls and planting tall trees?
360	There I would provide you food in plenty,
361	and clothe you in garments and give you sandals for your feet.
362	But since you have learned bad works, you will not wish
363	to go about work, but prefer to cower through the district,
364	so long as you can feed your insatiable belly.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Eurymachus, if only a contest of work were to arise between us two
367	in the season of spring, when the days are long,
368	in the grass, I with a well-curved sickle in hand,
369	and you with one like it, that we might test our work,
370	fasting until late dusk, and the grass were there;
371	or if again there were oxen to drive, the very best,
372	tawny, big, both well fed on grass,
373	of equal age, equal in load, whose strength is not feeble,
374	and it were a four-acre field, and the clod yielded to the plough;
375	then you would see me, whether I could cut a furrow unbroken.
376	Or if again the son of Kronos stirred up war from somewhere
377	today, and I had a shield and two spears
378	and an all-bronze helmet fitted to my temples,
379	then you would see me mingled among the foremost fighters,
380	and you would not speak reproaching me with my belly.
381	But you are very insolent, and your mind is cruel;
382	and you think yourself somehow great and mighty,
383	because you consort with few, and not good ones.
384	But if Odysseus were to come and reach his native land,
385	at once the doors, though very wide,
386	would be too narrow for you as you fled through the porch outside.
So he spoke, and Eurymachus was still more angered at heart,
and looking darkly at him addressed him with winged words:

Ah wretch, soon I shall bring evil on you for what you say
390	boldly among many men, and in your heart you are not at all
391	afraid; surely wine holds your wits, or always
392	such is your mind; so that you also babble vainly.
393	Are you out of your senses because you beat Irus the beggar?
So speaking he seized a footstool; but Odysseus
sat down at the knees of Amphinomus of Dulichium,
fearing Eurymachus; and he hit the cupbearer's hand,
the right one; and the jug fell to the ground with a clang,
and he with a groan fell on his back in the dust.
And the suitors roared through the shadowy halls,
and thus one would say, looking at his neighbour:

Would that the stranger had perished elsewhere in his wandering
402	before he came; he would not have raised so great a din for us.
403	But now we quarrel over beggars, and there will be no pleasure
404	in the good feast, since the worse things prevail.
And among them spoke the sacred might of Telemachus:

Strange men, you are mad, and no longer hide in your spirit
407	food and drink; some god is rousing you.
408	But having feasted well, go home and lie down,
409	when your spirit bids; I drive no one away.
So he spoke, and they all, biting their lips with their teeth,
marvelled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
And among them Amphinomus made a speech and said,
the shining son of Nisus, son of the lord Aretes:

O friends, no one would at a just saying
415	grow angry, assailing it with hostile words;
416	do not mistreat the stranger, nor any other
417	of the servants who are in the house of godly Odysseus.
418	But come, let the cupbearer begin the cups with a first pouring,
419	that having poured libations we may lie down, going home;
420	and the stranger let us leave in the halls of Odysseus
421	for Telemachus to care for; for to his house he came.
So he spoke, and he said a word pleasing to them all.
And for them the hero Mulius mixed the mixing-bowl,
the herald from Dulichium; he was Amphinomus' attendant;
and he served them all, standing by; and they, to the gods,
the blessed ones, poured libations and drank the honey-sweet wine.
But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their spirit wished,
they went to go, to lie down, each to his own house.
